item.title: It’s Time to Settle With Russia
item.description: In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

item.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability

  •  CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

CVE-2026-129713
A stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Mitigation
This vulnerability will be addressed in an upcoming Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series software release (version 5.5.x). In addition, Danfoss will remove the ability for users to disable Strict Mode in future software releases.

Mitigation
Until a software update is available, Danfoss recommends the following mitigations: * Follow the guidance provided in the product documentation and do not expose devices directly to the Internet or assign them public IP addresses. * Restrict remote access to affected devices by using a secure VPN or other protected network architecture. * Configure all affected devices to operate in Strict Mode, which provides enhanced security protections. * Use strong, unique passwords for all user accounts and administrative access. * For additional security recommendations and best practices see the Danfoss AK-SM 800 security guidance page: https://www.danfoss.com/en/service-and-support/downloads/dcs/adap-kool-software/ak-sm-800a/#tab-overview

Acknowledgments

  • Carlo Meijer of Midnight Blue reported CVE-2026-129713 to CISA.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

  • Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.
  • Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.
  • Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.

Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. item.title: CISA Adds 10 Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description:
CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability
  • CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability 

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

item.title: Defense Business Brief: Building warships; Drones; Neighborhood watch; and more...
How DARPA Challenged Teams to Bring Robots Into Disaster Triage
item.description:
On 5 November, 10 teams descended upon a 52-acre mock town in College Station, Texas called Disaster City. They were there for a nine-day competition to see how well teams of robots and humans could navigate simulated catastrophes, like a market ravaged by a tornado and a nighttime strike on a military base. At stake? US $2.5 million in prize money.

The scenarios were the final of the DARPA Triage Challenge, which the U.S. agency has been running for three years with the goal of saving more lives in urgent mass casualty events. Engineers from academia and industry have competed in elaborately staged mass casualty events, such as simulated combat zones and plane crash scenes. Teams spent years designing systems where autonomous ground robots and drones could help first responders find mock victims and decide the best way to care for them. “Triage is all about resources,” says Jeremy Pamplin, who managed the challenge for DARPA. Pamplin is a critical care physician and retired colonel who spent 28 years in the U.S. Army.

In mass casualty events, medics race to assess trauma with finite resources and limited time. Some victims need urgent help that medics can provide immediately, like tourniquets to halt bleeding. Some need evacuation and surgery. Others don’t need immediate help—either because their wounds are minimal enough, or because they’re so severe that a medic’s attention is better served elsewhere. Medics must prioritize who gets what care, but the line between each of these scenarios can be murky amid the rubble, frenzy, and heat of the moment.

It’s a difficult problem, and so the technologies developed in this competition could help real-world decisionmaking, says Gabriela Garcia Dolagaray, assistant medical director for emergency preparedness at Massachusetts General Hospital and the Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston. “Finding people can sometimes just be dangerous,” she says, “and getting a robust number of people to go out and search in a disaster area will take time.”

Trauma Technologies and the DARPA Triage Challenge

The Triage Challenge is the latest in a long DARPA legacy of running grand challenges to incentivize proof-of-concept development of important technologies. This particular challenge began as a program to quickly detect signs of trauma. DARPA imagined not only that drones and robots could find casualties, but that machine learning algorithms could assist in triage—which, at its core, is the process of assessing injuries and prioritizing care in a medical emergency.

Pamplin took over the competition in May 2025. “I have friends that still wake up in the middle of the night with these types of recollections and wondering if they did the right thing in the moment during a mass casualty incident,” Pamplin says. “That moves me. I would very much like to eliminate that uncertainty for them to the extent possible with this type of technology.”

He used his experience to make the competition increasingly elaborate and realistic. Year one featured a simulated convoy attack, and human participants sat in protective enclosures to avoid incidental run-ins with robots. In year two, when Pamplin took over the challenge, his team incorporated a full-size airplane fuselage to simulate a plane crash with dozens of victims. Organizers learned to recreate the physical environment of a disaster, and also the physical signs of injuries, like warm blood. Pamplin’s team visited a slaughterhouse with thermal cameras to study the temperature of blood spilling onto the ground. In the competition, they mimic that effect by heating water in a coffee pot and pouring it beside the body. This lets teams detect bleeding even at night.

A man performs a simulated triage as part of DARPA’s Triage Challenge finals. The program was designed to see how robots could assist in making triage decisions during an emergency.Paul Flacks/DARPA

“They always are throwing additional challenging things at us that you wouldn’t expect,” says Sam Colachis, a biomedical engineer at Battelle, an applied science and technology nonprofit in Columbus Ohio who led the organization’s DART team—short for “Drone-Assisted Rapid Triage”—in the competition.

The tactics required for successful triage are inherently multidisciplinary, says Derek Paley, a professor of aerospace engineering leading the University of Maryland’s team, RoboScout. Before 2022, Paley felt confident in his lab’s skills with autonomous navigation and algorithms, but he knew little about trauma medicine. “I didn’t even know what triage was,” he says.

Paley recruited colleagues in emergency medicine to help design his team’s approach and shape their tech. Before the Triage Challenge began, they felt like an underdog. “We kind of have a chip on our shoulder because we think we can play on the same field as these other teams…who’ve done grand challenges before,” Paley told Spectrum before the competition. They finished third in the first year of competition and second last year.

Each year’s competition began with four smaller trials that tested specific components of a robotic system. Teams first released their robots to locate as many casualties (a mix of live actors and manikins) as possible in 15 minutes. Next, they spent five minutes triaging injuries. Another trial presented teams with a fixed number of casualties in known locations to test how they assess trauma. Then, teams had ten minutes to collect vitals like pulse and breathing rate remotely from a few meters away. The top four teams moved into a semi-final where their robots worked with two human medics in simulated emergencies. And the two teams who performed best in four human-machine runs then moved to a 25-minute championship run.

Robots, Drones, and Autonomous Triage

When the teams arrived at Disaster City, they knew very little about the details of what awaited them. One self-funded team of college students from Delhi Technological University flew from India with 22 checked bags, each containing disembodied drones and wheeled robots they had handbuilt. Their team, Unmanned Aerial Systems, learned in the two prior years of the contest to simply expect the unexpected—from DARPA and their own systems. Upon arrival this year, they unzipped their luggage to find broken motors and chassis, camera parts, and missing screws. “We’re still trying to assemble everything before the competition,” Nishant Chandna calmly told IEEE Spectrum a couple days before the challenge. “It’s just part of it.”

Most teams in the challenge designed systems with a mix of ground robots and aerial drones. The student team from India built drones and wheeled robots to search for mock victims with onboard cameras and lidar.

But wheeled robots are problematic. They are more stable, cheaper, and easier to control than legged robots, but they struggle with stairs, entryways, and rough terrain littered with rubble. “We really needed a platform that could traverse those obstacles pretty easily,” says Eric Eaton, a machine learning scientist who led the University of Pennsylvania’s team, which began with drones and wheeled robots before expanding their fleet with four-legged Spot robots from Boston Dynamics that make it up stairs.

Paley’s RoboScout team opted for a strategy that involved sensing the scene from the ground. Their “dogs,” which were also Spot robots, listen for screaming victims, and help in one of the most difficult challenges in autonomous triage: quickly sensing vitals from with thermal cameras and radar. Millimeter-wave radar can detect the subtle movement of a pulse, and thermal cameras can measure breathing rates based on how breathing changes the temperature around a mouth and nose.

Battelle’s team had relied entirely on drones, even for measuring vital signs. Colachis says his team fuses inputs from multiple sensors including thermal, radar, and visual to calculate vitals. The team became almost notorious for their commitment to drones. “They keep threatening to bring a ground robot,” says RoboScout’s Paley, “but they always show up with drones.” For the first two years of the competition, it worked—Battelle won the first two rounds of the competition.

Members of the University of Maryland’s RoboScout team (on right) celebrate a successful run during the DARPA Triage Challenge finals.Paul Flacks/DARPA

RoboScout Wins DARPA Triage Grand Prize

During the final, organizers cast more than 500 actors to simulate casualties throughout the week. DARPA chose these actors to make obstacles like sensing vitals more realistic than previous years. Some were college students instructed to increase their heart and breathing rate on exercise bikes to simulate shock. Endurance athletes were instructed to lower their heart rates, simulating other injuries like airway failures. In the military base simulation, soldiers were running around a compound with alarms blaring. “Some of the explosions caused some of the medics to actually react to it,” Pamplin says, and “pull people to the ground so they didn’t get hit.”

Battelle did finally show up with a ground robot to help with measuring vitals remotely. But this time, the twice-champ finished second. The winner of DARPA’s Triage Challenge grand prize was the RoboScout team from the University of Maryland. The grand prize earned them $1.5 million.

After a perilous start slowed by software errors relating to the competition’s timer and Wi-Fi RoboScout rallied back through the final human-machine teaming portion. “We got hot at the right time,” Paley says. “It was pretty surreal.”

Other teams performed well despite having to improvise through engineering hiccups. Carnegie Mellon’s team, Chiron, struggled with a GPS error. After fixing it, they raced back and nearly made the final. The student team from Delhi didn’t meet a threshold for autonomous control in the competition, but they did earn the highest score in one sub-competition, winning $300,000.

“It’s an incredibly exciting challenge,” says Peter Fischer, trauma medical director with Washington Regional Medical Center in Fayetteville, Arkansas. “We struggle, especially with mass casualty incidents, in determining who the sickest patients are. In trauma, especially, you have to make sure that you triage these patients appropriately, so the sickest ones not only get the care the fastest, but get to the right place at the right time.”

Fischer was intrigued by a non-robotic branch of the competition, where two new teams excelled in predicting urgent care with the help of AI agents. He imagines these advances in robotics and algorithms could connect with additional data from hospitals. Triage algorithms could suggest where to take them to avoid overloading specific hospitals, he says, “That’s where we can really start to make a big difference.”

Although the competition has ended, the work continues. Several participants told IEEE Spectrum they plan to bring their teams’ AI algorithms elsewhere, such as hospital trauma bays, regional medical emergencies, and chemical weapon response.

For his part, DARPA’s Pamplin was most eager to compare performance to human medics without robots. A human-only team located 50 percent of casualties on average in daytime simulations; when paired with medics on one run of the same course, Maryland’s robots found every one. “That was the first time we’ve ever seen that,” he says. In the championship run, humans provided life-saving interventions to 25 percent of the mock casualties who needed them—RoboScout treated 74 percent. “That’s a couple lives,” Pamplin says. “That’s a couple humans that didn’t die that day.”

item.title: Pronunciamiento del Equipo Humanitario País sobre la protección de la población civil en Colombia - 25/11/2026
item.description:
Country: Colombia
Sources: El Equipo Humanitario País Colombia, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Bogotá, 25 de noviembre 2026

Las agencias de Naciones Unidas y las organizaciones humanitarias que integran el Equipo Humanitario de País (EHP) de Colombia notan con preocupación el deterioro de las condiciones de seguridad y sus consecuencias humanitarias, así como por la persistencia y expansión de graves riesgos para la población civil en distintas subregiones del país como el pacífico, nororiente, noroccidente y suroccidente del país.

El Equipo Humanitario País hace un llamado urgente a todos los actores armados para adoptar y fortalecer todas las medidas necesarias para prevenir daños y proteger a la población civil, respetando plenamente las normas del Derecho Internacional Humanitario (DIH), incluidos los principios de distinción, proporcionalidad y precaución. La población civil, los bienes de carácter civil y la infraestructura indispensable para su supervivencia deben ser protegidos en todo momento y permanecer al margen de las hostilidades.

Asimismo, el Equipo Humanitario País recuerda que la acción humanitaria se guía por los principios de humanidad, neutralidad, imparcialidad e independencia, que permiten brindar asistencia exclusivamente en función de las necesidades de las personas afectadas, sin discriminación. El respeto de estos principios por todas las partes es esencial para prevenir mayores afectaciones, preservar el espacio humanitario y generar las condiciones necesarias para llegar a las comunidades vulnerables que requieren asistencia y protección con el objetivo de salvar vidas. En este contexto, el Equipo Humanitario País hace un llamado a prevenir y eliminar las restricciones que puedan poner en riesgo a las comunidades o impedir la acción humanitaria, y a garantizar un acceso humanitario seguro,
oportuno, sostenido y sin obstáculos.

El Equipo Humanitario País reafirma su compromiso de continuar acompañando de manera coordinada a las comunidades afectadas y fortaleciendo las acciones de prevención y respuesta humanitaria, sobre la base de los principios humanitarios y del respeto del Derecho Internacional Humanitario, como se ha realizado en las últimas décadas.

Asimismo, reiteran su disposición a contribuir a generar las condiciones necesarias para prevenir nuevas afectaciones, promover la protección de la población civil y asegurar que la asistencia humanitaria llegue de manera segura a quienes más la necesitan.

item.title: World: How can we support survivors of gender-based violence?
item.description:
Country: World
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

In conflict and crisis settings, up to 70% of women face some form of violence. Recognizing this reality, designing solutions to protect them, and committing to ways of working that do not perpetuate threats to women's lives and well-being is one of our priorities. In this article, we share recommendations for delivering a safe, dignified humanitarian response that avoids revictimization.

When an emergency or disaster strikes, institutional and community support networks weaken, livelihoods are disrupted, and pre-existing inequalities and vulnerabilities deepen. As a result, in crisis-affected settings, up to 70% of women experience violence, nearly double the rate recorded outside crisis zones.

The challenge is even more urgent given global gaps in violence prevention and care. In 2025 alone, 50% of survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) were reported to lack access to essential services such as safe spaces, health care, psychosocial support, protection, or legal assistance, leaving at least one million women and girls without vital care.

At the same time, women's organizations report an increase in demand for services since January 2025 and indicate that most can no longer meet current levels of need at a time marked by humanitarian funding cuts.

During the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, running from November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, to December 10, International Human Rights Day, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) reaffirms its priority of placing the protection of survivors at the centre of every emergency response.

Humanitarian teams must operate on the premise that gender-based violence occurs in every crisis and must take protective measures consistent with humanitarian standards, whether or not formal reports or concrete evidence exist.

Recognizing all forms of violence and acting locally

A life free from violence, gender equality, and the equitable sharing of family responsibilities between women and men are essential for personal and social well-being. To prevent and respond effectively, the first practical step is recognizing that gender-based violence takes many forms, often hidden from view:

  • Sexual violence and sexual abuse.
  • Domestic or intimate partner violence.
  • Economic violence (control or deprivation of financial resources).
  • Forced or child marriage.
  • Forced prostitution and sexual exploitation.

Within Red Cross and Red Crescent volunteering spaces worldwide, women's leadership and expertise are indispensable to building safe and effective protection systems.

Prevention begins at the very design stage of operations, from setting up safe spaces for women, children, and LGBTQIA+ populations, to ensuring dignified supplies for menstrual health management, mapping safe referral pathways, and promoting diverse representation at all levels of leadership.

5 keys to supporting survivors with dignity and doing no harm

All actions to address gender-based violence must be guided by the "do no harm" principle and remain survivor-centred. If someone discloses an experience of violence, these five guidelines steer an ethical and safe initial response:

1. Listen without judging or interrupting

To ensure the person's comfort and safety, provide a private, confidential, and safe space. Listen attentively as part of psychological first aid, without offering opinions, questioning, or judging what happened. Allow the person to express their emotions freely, without minimizing their feelings or giving unsolicited advice.

2. Ask for consent and respect confidentiality

Humanitarian personnel must respect the survivor's pace and avoid pressuring them to share more than they wish. Asking them to repeat their story over and over, or conducting detailed questioning without specialized training, causes revictimization. Humanitarian work is not about investigating, but about supporting and facilitating safe referrals. Furthermore, personal data must never be shared, nor an adult case referred, without the survivor's express and informed consent, unless there is an imminent threat to life.

3. Adapt the environment and ensure inclusion

When supporting a survivor of gender-based violence, we must guarantee affirmative, accessible, and bias-free treatment, ensuring that no one is left unprotected.

Women and girls with disabilities experience higher rates of violence and often have fewer accessible services available to them. We can remove physical and communication barriers by using clear language, visual aids, or interpreters when needed, and by actively involving them in designing solutions.

We must also avoid making assumptions about a person's gender or sexual orientation, and always use the name and pronouns they indicate.

Ensuring inclusion means enabling the person to participate actively in every decision regarding their process, upholding their rights, wishes, and the safety of their family.

4. Make safe referrals for medical emergencies

Sexual violence is a medical emergency that requires care within the first 72 hours to prevent sexually transmitted infections (including HIV), unintended pregnancies, and physical or psychological harm. Sharing reliable, accessible information about medical, psychosocial, legal, and economic support services available in the community is part of health care. This action does not obligate health personnel to file a legal report, but it connects the person with specialized networks safely and confidentially.

5. Protect children and adolescents

Protecting children and adolescents is a shared responsibility and requires strict protocols to avoid exposing them to further harm.

In a private and safe environment, we must ensure the child or adolescent knows we believe them and that what happened was not their fault.

If there is imminent danger, we must move the child or adolescent away from the perpetrator, without confronting the perpetrator directly to avoid greater risks, and immediately alert the relevant child protection and safety authorities.

Subsequently, we must refer the case to official child protection agencies and specialized health and psychological first aid services, avoiding in-depth interviews that could cause revictimization.

Humanitarian personnel must also keep the family or safe support network accompanied and informed throughout the entire process.

Prevention and care from the field

Protecting communities requires humanitarian operations to be safe environments of high integrity. The IFRC enforces a strict Zero Tolerance policy against any form of harassment, discrimination, sexual exploitation, or abuse.

Safeguarding rules are non-negotiable for all staff and volunteers:

  • Zero tolerance for any sexual activity with children and adolescents.
  • Offering money, employment, goods, services, or humanitarian assistance in exchange for sexual favours is strictly prohibited.
  • Sexual relationships between humanitarian personnel and the people they assist, as well as any misuse of position or hierarchy, are prohibited.

Any suspicion of misconduct, sexual exploitation and abuse, harassment, or integrity violations can be reported safely and confidentially through the IFRC Integrity Line at www.ifrc.integrityline.org, by email at [email protected], or by calling toll-free at +41 800 437 272.

An urgent call to action

Violence against women and girls is a human rights violation for which there is no excuse. To reverse this crisis, the IFRC network calls on governments, donors, and partner organizations to act on five priority fronts:

  • Maintain essential services and safeguard sustained funding.
  • Ensure justice and accountability to end impunity.
  • Strengthen locally led prevention and response by investing in women's leadership.
  • Integrate protection into every stage of humanitarian action.

Human rights belong to everyone; safety must too. Ending violence against women and girls is a collective effort that begins with believing, listening without prejudice, and ensuring that every space of support is truly safe and dignified.

item.title: World: ¿Cómo acompañar a sobrevivientes de violencia basada en género?
item.description:
Country: World
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

En contextos de conflicto y crisis, hasta el 70 % de las mujeres enfrenta algún tipo de violencia. Reconocer esta realidad, diseñar soluciones para protegerlas y apostar por formas de trabajo que no perpetúen las amenazas contra la vida y el bienestar de las mujeres es una de nuestras prioridades. En este artículo compartimos recomendaciones para ofrecer una respuesta humanitaria segura, digna y sin revictimización.

Cuando ocurre una emergencia o un desastre, las redes de apoyo institucional y comunitario se debilitan, los medios de vida se interrumpen y las desigualdades y vulnerabilidades previas se agudizan. Como resultado, en entornos afectados por crisis, hasta el 70 % de las mujeres enfrenta situaciones de violencia, casi el doble de la tasa registrada fuera de las zonas de crisis.

El desafío es aún más urgente ante las brechas globales de prevención y atención a la violencia. Solo en 2025, se reportó que el 50% de las personas sobrevivientes de violencia basada en género (VBG) no tuvo acceso a servicios esenciales como espacios seguros, atención médica, apoyo psicosocial, protección o asistencia legal, dejando al menos a un millón de mujeres y niñas sin atención vital.

Al mismo tiempo, las organizaciones de mujeres reportan un aumento en la demanda de servicios desde enero de 2025 e indican que la mayoría ya no logran cubrir los niveles actuales de necesidad en un momento marcado por recortes al financiamiento humanitario.

En los 16 Días de Activismo contra la Violencia de Género, que se extienden del 25 de noviembre, Día Internacional de la Eliminación de la Violencia contra la Mujer, al 10 de diciembre, Día de los Derechos Humanos, la Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (IFRC) reafirma la prioridad de poner en el centro la protección de las sobrevivientes en cada respuesta de emergencia.

Los equipos humanitarios deben actuar bajo la premisa de que la violencia basada en género ocurre en toda crisis y deben tomar medidas de protección coherentes con las normas humanitarias, existan o no denuncias o pruebas concretas.

Reconocer todas las caras de la violencia y actuar desde lo local

Una vida libre de violencia, la igualdad de género y el reparto equitativo de las responsabilidades familiares entre hombres y mujeres son esenciales para el bienestar personal y social. Para prevenir y responder de forma efectiva, el primer paso práctico es reconocer que la violencia basada en género adopta múltiples formas, muchas veces invisibilizadas:

  • Violencia sexual y abuso sexual.
  • Violencia doméstica o intrafamiliar.
  • Violencia económica (control o privación de recursos financieros).
  • Matrimonio forzado o precoz.
  • Prostitución forzada y explotación sexual.

Dentro de los espacios de voluntariado de la Cruz Roja y la Media Luna Roja en todo el mundo, el liderazgo y la experiencia de las mujeres son indispensables para construir sistemas de protección seguros y eficaces.

La prevención comienza desde el diseño mismo de las operaciones, desde habilitar espacios seguros para mujeres, niñez y poblaciones LGBTQIA+, hasta garantizar insumos dignos para la gestión de la salud menstrual, mapear rutas de derivación segura e impulsar la representación diversa en todos los niveles de liderazgo.

5 claves para acompañar con dignidad y no hacer daño

Todas las acciones para abordar la violencia basada en género deben regirse por el principio de no hacer daño y estar centradas en la persona sobreviviente. Si una persona comparte una situación de violencia, estas cinco pautas guían una primera respuesta ética y segura:

1. Escuchar sin juzgar ni interrumpir

Para asegurar la comodidad y seguridad de la persona, es importante habilitar un espacio privado, confidencial y seguro. Escuche con atención como parte de los primeros auxilios psicológicos, sin emitir opiniones, cuestionamientos ni juicios sobre lo ocurrido. Permita que la persona exprese sus emociones libremente, sin minimizar sus sentimientos ni darle consejos no solicitados.

2. Pedir consentimiento y respetar la confidencialidad

El personal humanitario debe respetar los tiempos de la persona sobreviviente y evitar presionarla para que cuente más de lo que desea. Pedirle que repita su relato una y otra vez, o hacer interrogatorios detallados sin ser personal especializado genera revictimización. La labor humanitaria no es investigar, sino acompañar y facilitar derivaciones seguras. Además, nunca se deben compartir los datos ni derivar un caso adulto sin su consentimiento expreso e informado, salvo que exista un riesgo vital inminente.

3. Adaptar el entorno y asegurar la inclusión

Cuando acompañamos a una persona que ha sobrevivido a violencia de género debemos garantizar un trato afirmativo, accesible y libre de prejuicios, asegurando que ninguna persona esté desprotegida.

Las mujeres y niñas con discapacidad enfrentan tasas más altas de violencia y suelen contar con menos servicios adaptados. Podemos eliminar barreras físicas y comunicacionales utilizando lenguaje claro, apoyo visual o intérpretes si es necesario, e involucrpandoles activamente en el diseño de las soluciones.

También debemos evitar suposiciones sobre el género u orientación sexual de la persona, y utilizar siempre el nombre y los pronombres que la persona indique.

Asegurar la inclusión implica facilitar que la persona se involucre activamente en cada decisión sobre su proceso, ejerciendo sus derechos, deseos y la seguridad de su familia.

4. Realizar derivaciones seguras de emergencias médicas

La violencia sexual es una emergencia médica que requiere atención en las primeras 72 horas para prevenir infecciones de transmisión sexual (incluido el VIH), embarazos no deseados y secuelas físicas o psicológicas. Compartir información confiable y accesible sobre los servicios médicos, psicosociales, legales y de apoyo económico disponibles en la comunidad, es parte de la atención en salud. Esta acción no condiciona al personal de salud a presentar una denuncia, pero sí conecta a la persona con redes especializadas de forma segura y confidencial.

5. Proteger a la niñez y adolescencia

La protección de la niñez y la adolescencia es una responsabilidad compartida y exige protocolos estrictos para no exponer a la niñez y la adolescencia a mayores riesgos.

En un entorno privado y seguro, debemos asegurarnos de que la persona menor de edad sepa que vamos a creer en su palabra y que sabemos que no fue su culpa.

Si existe peligro inminente, debemos resguardar al niño, niña o adolescente lejos de la persona agresora, sin confrontarla directamente para evitar riesgos mayores y activa de inmediato las alertas ante las autoridades de protección y seguridad correspondientes.

Posteriormente debemos derivar el caso hacia los organismos oficiales de protección de la infancia y servicios especializados de salud y primeros auxilios psicológicos, evitando entrevistas profundas que puedan causar revictimización.

El personal humanitario también debe mantener acompañada e informada a la familia o red segura durante todo el proceso.

Prevención y cuidados desde el terreno

Proteger a las comunidades exige que las operaciones humanitarias sean un entorno íntegro y seguro. En la IFRC rige una política estricta de Tolerancia Cero frente a cualquier forma de acoso, discriminación, explotación o abuso sexual.

Las reglas de salvaguarda son innegociables para todo el personal y el voluntariado:

  • Cero tolerancia a cualquier actividad sexual con niños, niñas y adolescentes.
  • Está estrictamente prohibido ofrecer dinero, empleo, bienes, servicios o asistencia humanitaria a cambio de favores sexuales.
  • No se permiten relaciones sexuales entre el personal humanitario y las personas atendidas, ni el uso indebido del cargo o la jerarquía.

Cualquier sospecha de conducta indebida, explotación, abuso sexual, acoso o vulneración de la integridad puede reportarse de forma segura y confidencial a través de la línea de integridad de la IFRC en www.ifrc.integrityline.org, al correo electrónico [email protected] o llamando de manera gratuita al +41 800 437 272.

Un llamado urgente a la acción

La violencia contra las mujeres y las niñas es una violación de los derechos humanos para la que no existe excusa. Para revertir esta crisis, la red de la IFRC hace un llamado a gobiernos, donantes y organizaciones aliadas a actuar en cinco frentes prioritarios:

  • Proteger a las personas sobrevivientes.
  • Mantener los servicios esenciales y salvaguardar su financiamiento sostenido.
  • Garantizar la justicia y la rendición de cuentas para poner fin a la impunidad.
  • Fortalecer la prevención y respuesta lideradas localmente, invirtiendo en el liderazgo de las mujeres.
  • Integrar la protección en cada etapa de la acción humanitaria.

Los derechos humanos pertenecen a todas las personas; la seguridad también debe serlo. Erradicar la violencia contra las mujeres y las niñas es una tarea colectiva que empieza por creer, escuchar sin prejuicios y garantizar que cada espacio de apoyo sea verdaderamente seguro y digno.

item.title: From Rainfall Forecasts to Anticipatory Action: A Flood Digital Twin at Work in Dolo Ado, Ethiopia (November 2026)
item.description:
Country: Ethiopia
Source: CGIAR

Please refer to the attached file.

Citation

Haile, Alemseged Tamiru, Eden Seifu Gebre, Getahun Kebede Mengistie, Abel Negussie Alemu, and Hugox Retief. 2026. From Rainfall Forecasts to Anticipatory Action: A Flood Digital Twin at Work in Dolo Ado, Ethiopia. International Water Management Institute.

Abstract/Description

Flood Early Warning Bulletins translate forecasts into clear, timely, actionable information for preparedness, anticipatory action, and emergency response. By presenting expected conditions, potential impacts, and recommended actions in a standard format, they help government agencies, humanitarian organizations, and at-risk communities coordinate decisions before floods occur. Yet fragmented datasets, disconnected modelling workflows, and manual processes often delay bulletins and shorten the time available to protect lives, livelihoods, and infrastructure.

To address this gap, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), national government institutions, and development partners developed the Dolo Ado Digital Twin-based Flood Early Warning System. It creates a digital replica of the floodplain, enables two-way data exchange with communities, and integrates global databases, field surveys, and district data. HEC-HMS converts rainfall forecasts into flood forecasts, while HEC-RAS simulates likely inundation, including water depth and flood duration across the river and floodplain.

A key achievement is the co-created Flood Early Warning Bulletin, refined by stakeholders through consultations, co-design workshops, technical training, and continuous feedback. An automated workflow rapidly converts reliable Digital Twin forecasts into standardized warnings, with content, visuals, terminology, and format tailored to operational needs. The bulletin enables government agencies, humanitarian organizations, and disaster risk management authorities to make timely, coordinated decisions before and during floods.

item.title: Brazil: PAHO calls for stronger surveillance amid increase in mpox cases in the Americas
item.description:
Countries: Brazil, World
Source: Pan American Health Organization

Washington, D.C., 25 November 2026 (PAHO) – The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) is urging countries in the Americas to strengthen surveillance, laboratory capacity and prevention measures, including vaccination, in response to a surge in mpox cases in several countries of the Region.

In an Epidemiological Alert issued on 24 November, PAHO highlights an increase in cases since epidemiological week 39 of 2026, primarily in Brazil, alongside the growing detection of mpox clade Ib in the Region.

From January to November 2026, 13 countries reported 3,269 confirmed cases and four deaths. Since 2022, 76,084 cases and 202 deaths have been reported across 31 countries and territories in the Americas. Brazil has reported 1,325 cases in 2026, including one death, with an increase since September.

Mpox continues to disproportionately affect men who have sex with men. Of the 114 reported mpox deaths for which HIV status was known, 111 (97%) were among people with HIV.

PAHO is urging health authorities to strengthen epidemiological and genomic surveillance to ensure timely detection and investigation of cases, monitor changes in transmission patterns, and reinforce targeted prevention and control measures, including vaccination, particularly among populations at increased risk.

What is mpox and how can it be prevented?

Mpox is an infectious disease caused by the mpox virus. It can spread through close physical contact with someone who has the infection, including skin-to-skin and intimate contact, as well as through contact with contaminated materials such as clothing and bedding.

Symptoms commonly include a skin rash or lesions, fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue and swollen lymph nodes. The rash can appear on the face, hands, feet, genital and anal areas, and inside the mouth or throat.

Anyone who develops an unexplained rash or other symptoms consistent with mpox should seek medical advice and testing, particularly if they have had close contact with someone who may have the infection.

Vaccination is recommended for groups at high risk of infection, based on each country's epidemiological situation. Travelers belonging to higher-risk groups are advised to seek vaccination before traveling to areas with active transmission. Vaccination should complement, not replace, other prevention measures.

Background

On 14 August 2024, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared mpox a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) following the international spread of cases and the risk of sustained transmission. The emergency designation was lifted on 5 September 2025, after the global impact of the outbreak had decreased and surveillance and response capacities had strengthened.

The end of the PHEIC did not mean that mpox had ceased to pose a public health risk. The virus continues to circulate, with different clades detected in several regions and new transmission patterns emerging. PAHO's latest alert underscores the importance of maintaining surveillance and preparedness to detect and respond to cases promptly.

item.title: Brazil: ACNUR agradece la contribución de Japón para apoyar a las personas refugiadas y desplazadas por la fuerza en Brasil y Ecuador
item.description:
Countries: Brazil, Ecuador, Japan
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

CIUDAD DE PANAMÁ – ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, acoge con satisfacción la generosa contribución de 2 millones de dólares estadounidenses (USD) del Gobierno de Japón para apoyar el proyecto “Fortalecimiento de la Protección y Promoción de la Inclusión Socioeconómica de las Personas Desplazadas”, un proyecto regional que fortalecerá la protección, ampliará el acceso a derechos y servicios, y promoverá la inclusión socioeconómica de las personas refugiadas y desplazadas por la fuerza en Brasil y Ecuador.

La financiación apoyará actividades durante un período de 12 meses, con las que se prevé beneficiar a aproximadamente 19.500 personas refugiadas y otras personas con necesidades de protección internacional, así como a miembros de las comunidades de acogida, mediante iniciativas diseñadas para fortalecer los sistemas de protección, ampliar las oportunidades económicas y reforzar la capacidad de las autoridades locales y las comunidades que responden al desplazamiento.

“ACNUR agradece profundamente al Gobierno y al pueblo de Japón por su constante solidaridad y apoyo”, afirmó Isabel Márquez, Directora Regional de ACNUR para las Américas. “En un momento en que muchas personas refugiadas y desplazadas por la fuerza siguen enfrentando riesgos de protección y obstáculos para su inclusión, la contribución de Japón ayudará a generar mayores oportunidades de seguridad, autosuficiencia y dignidad, al tiempo que fortalecerá a las comunidades que las acogen”.

El proyecto se articula en torno a tres pilares complementarios: el fortalecimiento de los sistemas de asilo y del acceso a la protección; la promoción de la estabilización y la inclusión socioeconómica; y el refuerzo de la capacidad de municipios y comunidades que se encuentran en la primera línea de recepción y apoyo a las poblaciones desplazadas.

En Brasil, el proyecto apoyará la mejora del acceso a la protección y la documentación, ampliará las oportunidades de medios de vida y empleabilidad, y fortalecerá los servicios municipales y los mecanismos comunitarios de protección en las zonas que acogen a importantes poblaciones refugiadas. La iniciativa también respaldará los esfuerzos para facilitar el acceso a oportunidades económicas sostenibles y promover la integración local.

En Ecuador, el proyecto fortalecerá el acceso a los servicios de asilo y protección, mejorará la gestión de casos y las derivaciones hacia servicios esenciales, promoverá el emprendimiento y la inclusión económica, y apoyará a los gobiernos locales y organizaciones comunitarias que desempeñan un papel fundamental en el fortalecimiento de la cohesión social y la resiliencia.

La iniciativa refleja el compromiso sostenido Japón con la promoción de la seguridad humana y el apoyo a soluciones duraderas para las poblaciones desplazadas por la fuerza. A través de contribuciones específicas en sistemas de protección, medios de vida y capacidades locales, el proyecto contribuirá a que las personas refugiadas y desplazadas por la fuerza reconstruyan sus vidas y aporten de manera positiva a las comunidades que las acogen.

En toda la región de las Américas, el desplazamiento continúa siendo impulsado por la violencia, la inseguridad, las violaciones de los derechos humanos, las presiones económicas y los impactos relacionados con el clima. La mayoría de las personas refugiadas y desplazadas por la fuerza permanecen dentro de la región, buscando seguridad y oportunidades en países vecinos. Fortalecer los sistemas nacionales de protección sigue siendo fundamental para garantizar la protección, fomentar la autosuficiencia y promover la convivencia pacífica en las comunidades afectadas por el desplazamiento.
